passage: On the pavement outside their building in Toronto, Leila was drawing a whale with blue chalk. Yuki stopped hopping and stared. The whale had a curly spout and a tiny smiling eye. "Your drawing is so good," Yuki said, bouncing on her toes. Leila grinned and added three bubbles. Yuki looked at her own chalk sun, a wobbly orange circle, and did not rub it out. "Will you show me how the tail curls?" Leila took Yuki's hand and moved it slowly along the ground. Soon a second, smaller whale swam beside the first.

qa.q: What was Leila drawing with blue chalk?
qa.a: Leila was drawing a whale with a curly spout and a tiny smiling eye.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she looked at the whale?
qa.a: Yuki felt happy and admiring; she bounced on her toes and praised it, and she stayed curious instead of jealous about her own wobbly sun.

qa.q: What small step turned Yuki's praise into learning?
qa.a: She asked Leila to show her how the tail curls, so the two of them ended up drawing a second whale together. 🙂

qa.q: How might Leila see Yuki's kind words?
qa.a: Leila probably felt pleased and proud, which made sharing the chalk trick feel easy and fun.

grounding: A young child admires a friend's drawing without envy and asks to be shown how it was done.

passage: At the daycare art table, Charu's paper was still empty. Beside her, Preeti was colouring a peacock with a tail full of green and purple eyes. Charu put down her crayon and leaned close. "Preeti, your drawing is so good!" she said, and her smile went right up to her cheeks. Preeti sat up taller. "It's for my Nani." Charu tapped the tail. "How did you make the round eyes? Will you show me?" Preeti drew one small circle on Charu's paper. Charu copied it, then another, and another. By snack time Charu had a peacock of her own.

qa.q: Who was Preeti's peacock drawing for?
qa.a: Preeti said the peacock was for her Nani.

qa.q: How can you tell Charu felt glad rather than jealous?
qa.a: She smiled right up to her cheeks while praising Preeti, then leaned in eager to learn, even though her own paper was still empty.

qa.q: What could a daycare teacher notice and encourage here?
qa.a: The teacher could name Charu's kind words and her question, and let the two friends keep drawing side by side.

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti when Charu praises her peacock?
qa.a: Preeti feels proud and noticed; she sits up taller and happily draws a circle to teach Charu.

grounding: A young child praises a friend's drawing warmly and asks to learn the trick, admiring without envy.

passage:
"I want the laddoo NOW!"
"Not before dinner, Sahil," said his dad, Farhan. "After dal and rice, you can have one."
"NOW!" Sahil screamed and flung himself onto the rug. His legs kicked. He grabbed a cushion to throw.
Farhan sat down on the floor, not too close. "You're very angry. Cushions stay on the sofa. I'm here."
"I hate dinner!"
"I know. The laddoo is still for after. Want to blow out my finger candles with me?"
Sahil glared. Then he blew, once, twice. His kicking slowed. The cushion slid out of his hand.

qa.q: Where did Sahil fling himself when he screamed?
qa.a: Sahil flung himself onto the rug and his legs kicked.

qa.q: What does Sahil's kicking and screaming suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He is furious and overwhelmed, as if his body is too big for the anger, so it comes out in kicks and a thrown cushion.

qa.q: Which choice of Farhan's helped most, and why?
qa.a: He stayed calm, kept the laddoo rule and offered finger-candle breaths, so Sahil had a way to settle without winning by screaming.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel sitting on the floor during the tantrum?
qa.a: Farhan may feel tired and tested but steady, holding the limit while staying close enough for Sahil to feel safe.

grounding: A small child's anger about sweets bursts into a tantrum, and a calm parent keeps the limit and helps him breathe.

passage:
Diary note for Yogesh's class teacher, from his papa, Amandeep.
Pick-up yesterday was hard. At the sweet shop by the gate, I said no to jalebi because we had cake at home. Yogesh screamed, dropped to the floor and threw his water bottle at the counter. I picked the bottle up, knelt beside him and said, "You're angry. Throwing is not okay. Let's breathe." We counted five slow breaths together. He cried on my shoulder, then walked home holding my hand. He may be tired today. 🙏

qa.q: What did Yogesh throw at the sweet shop?
qa.a: Yogesh threw his water bottle at the counter.

qa.q: How was Yogesh feeling when he dropped to the floor?
qa.a: He was furious and overwhelmed about the jalebi, and the anger was too big for him to hold, so it came out as screaming and throwing.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that a wise grown-up would do?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named the anger, said throwing was not okay and breathed with Yogesh, without giving in about the jalebi.

qa.q: If you were Yogesh's class teacher, what would you want to know from this note?
qa.a: That Yogesh had a hard evening, so the teacher can be gentle with him if he seems tired or cranky today.

grounding: A preschooler's anger about sweets becomes a tantrum with throwing, and a parent stays calm, holds the limit and helps him breathe.

passage: The colony lights had come on. Ojas was still on the slide. "Five more minutes, Mumma!" Usha shook her head. "It's dark. We're going home." Ojas stamped and began to cry. A neighbour looked over from the gate. Usha crouched in front of him. "I know you are upset. The answer is still no." Her voice was soft and did not wobble. Ojas cried a little longer, then held out his arms. Usha picked him up. At home, Ojas put his muddy shoes by the door and asked if they could come back early tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Usha say they had to go home?
qa.a: Usha said it was dark, and the colony lights had come on.

qa.q: What does Ojas holding out his arms suggest he felt?
qa.a: His anger was passing and he felt safe with his mother, even though she had not changed her answer.

qa.q: What made Usha's limit work well?
qa.a: She crouched to his level, named his upset and kept the same no in a soft, steady voice, so the rule did not break.

qa.q: How might Usha feel with a neighbour watching?
qa.a: She might feel a little self-conscious, but she chose to stay calm and focus on Ojas instead of giving in to end the scene.

grounding: A parent stays calm and keeps a limit, and the child settles because the rule stays steady and loving.

passage:
"Papa, I'm wearing my sparkly sandals!"
"Not today, Trisha. It's raining. Wellies."
"But sparkly!"
"I know you are upset. The answer is still no."
"You're not fair!" Trisha threw herself on the stairs and cried.
Joseph sat one step below her. "Big feeling, hmm? I'll wait."
"Can the sandals come in my bag?"
"They can come in the bag. Wellies on the feet."
Trisha sniffed. She pulled on one welly, then the other. "Can I jump in the puddles?"
Joseph laughed. "That's what wellies are for."

qa.q: What did Joseph say could go in the bag?
qa.a: Joseph said the sparkly sandals could come in the bag, but wellies had to go on her feet.

qa.q: How was Trisha feeling when she threw herself on the stairs?
qa.a: She was upset and cross that her father would not let her wear the sparkly sandals in the rain.

qa.q: What small step helped Trisha move on from her big feeling?
qa.a: Joseph waited calmly and let the sandals come in her bag, which gave her something to hold onto while the rule stayed firm. 😊

qa.q: How does Joseph see Trisha's crying on the stairs?
qa.a: He sees it as a big feeling that will pass, so he waits nearby instead of shouting or giving in.

grounding: A child feels upset about a rule, but a calm and steady no from a parent helps her settle and accept it.

passage:
In the courtyard, Farida kicked her slippers off and wailed. She wanted to go to the fair with the older cousins. Her Ammi, Salma, shouted, "Stop that noise or I'll lock you in the room!" Farida went silent. Her lip shook and she pressed herself against the wall.
That evening, Salma sat down beside her on the charpai. "I was loud and I scared you. I'm sorry. You're too small for the fair crowd, that's why I said no. Big feelings aren't your fault." She held out her arms. Farida crept into them.

qa.q: What did Salma threaten when Farida wailed?
qa.a: Salma shouted that she would lock Farida in the room if she did not stop the noise.

qa.q: What does Farida's shaking lip suggest she felt after the shout?
qa.a: She felt frightened; she stopped crying out of fear, not because she understood why she could not go.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Salma do to fix it?
qa.a: The shouting and threat scared Farida silent; later Salma apologised, explained the reason and hugged her, which helped repair things.

qa.q: How might Salma feel sitting on the charpai that evening?
qa.a: Salma probably felt sorry and a bit guilty about scaring her daughter, and wanted Farida to feel safe with her again.

grounding: A parent shouts and threatens during a tantrum, the child is frightened into silence, and a later hug and explanation repair it.

passage:
Rain streamed down the bus shelter in Manchester. Anders lay on the wet ground, howling because the bus was late and his feet were cold. His dad, Chidi, snapped, "Get up now or no park for a week!" Anders froze. He stopped crying, but he stared at his boots and would not look up.
On the bus, Chidi pulled him onto his lap. "I shouted, and that was scary. Being cold and tired is hard. It's not your fault you felt so big inside." Anders leaned in and let out a long, shaky breath.

qa.q: Why was Anders howling at the bus shelter?
qa.a: Anders was howling because the bus was late and his feet were cold.

qa.q: How can you tell Anders was frightened after Chidi snapped?
qa.a: He froze, stopped crying and stared at his boots without looking up, which shows fear rather than calm.

qa.q: How could a parent handle a moment like the bus shelter differently?
qa.a: They could stay calm, name that Anders was cold and tired, and offer a cuddle or a game while waiting, instead of a threat.

qa.q: What is it like for Chidi when he pulls Anders onto his lap?
qa.a: Chidi likely feels sorry about snapping and relieved to have a chance to explain and make Anders feel safe again.

grounding: A parent's shout and threat frighten a child out of a tantrum, and a calmer hug and explanation later help him feel safe.

passage: After the shouting at the vegetable market, Noor and her mother, Devika, walked next door to the clinic for Noor's check-up. In the waiting room, Noor climbed onto the chair and pushed her face into her knees. She had knocked over a basket of tomatoes. People had stared. "Am I bad, Mama?" she whispered. Devika stroked her hair. "You were upset. It is over. Let us fix it. After the doctor, we'll help the tomato uncle stack them again." Noor peeped out from behind her knees.

qa.q: What had Noor knocked over at the market?
qa.a: Noor had knocked over a basket of tomatoes.

qa.q: Why did Noor push her face into her knees?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and sorry about the tantrum and the people staring, and worried she was bad.

qa.q: What did Devika say that helped the shame pass?
qa.a: She said Noor was upset, that it was over, and offered a way to fix it by helping stack the tomatoes.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had said Noor was a bad girl?
qa.a: Noor's shame would stick; she might keep hiding and believe she was bad instead of learning she could make things right.

grounding: A child hides her face in shame after a market tantrum, and her parent comforts her and offers a way to repair it.

passage:
Saturday: At the fruit stall, Siddharth screamed for mangoes and knocked a pile of lemons into the gutter. On the walk home, he hid his face in Ishita's dupatta.
Sunday: When Papa said "market", Siddharth ran under the bed. Ishita lay on the floor to see him. "You were upset. It is over. Let us fix it." Together they drew a sorry card with yellow lemons.
Next Saturday: Siddharth handed the card to the fruit seller. She laughed and gave him a lemon to hold. He walked home swinging it.

qa.q: What did Siddharth knock into the gutter?
qa.a: Siddharth knocked a pile of lemons into the gutter.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth run under the bed on Sunday?
qa.a: He still felt ashamed and embarrassed about the tantrum, so even the word market made him want to hide.

qa.q: Which step helped Siddharth stop hiding?
qa.a: Ishita's calm words and the sorry card gave him a way to fix things, so he could face the fruit seller again.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller see Siddharth's card?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and amused; she laughs and gives him a lemon, showing the tantrum is forgiven.

grounding: Over a week, a child's shame after a market tantrum eases when his parent calls it over and helps him make amends.

passage:
Note for Divyansh's parents, from his teacher at Little Steps.
Today Chaitanya knocked down Divyansh's block tower by accident. Divyansh's face went red and his fists were tight. Then he picked up the class teddy, hugged it hard and blew three "birthday candle" breaths, like we practised. He said, "I am angry!" in a big voice. I said, "You told us with words." He smiled and rebuilt his tower. 🌟 He was so proud he showed me the teddy twice. Please praise him at home!

qa.q: What did Divyansh hug after his tower fell?
qa.a: He picked up the class teddy and hugged it hard.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after he calmed down?
qa.a: He felt proud; he smiled, rebuilt his tower and showed the teddy to his teacher twice.

qa.q: What small calming actions did Divyansh use?
qa.a: He hugged the teddy, blew three birthday candle breaths and said out loud that he was angry.

qa.q: What is it like for Chaitanya when Divyansh stays calm?
qa.a: Chaitanya is spared a fight or blame for an accident, and the two can go back to playing blocks.

grounding: A preschooler uses a teddy hug, candle breaths and naming his anger to calm down, and feels proud afterwards.

passage: The wind tore Tanvir's paper kite on the thorn bush behind the gurdwara. He stamped. He wanted to shout at the wind. His didi, Baljeet, knelt on the dusty path. "Where's Bhalu?" Tanvir pulled the old cloth bear from his kurta pocket and squeezed it. "Birthday candles," Baljeet said. Tanvir puffed out one, two, three. "I am angry," he said. "The wind broke it." Baljeet nodded. His shoulders came down. He looked at the kite and then grinned. "I did it, Didi. I calmed down all by myself."

qa.q: Where did the wind tear Tanvir's kite?
qa.a: The wind tore it on the thorn bush behind the gurdwara.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he said, "I did it, Didi"?
qa.a: He felt proud of himself for calming down, after first feeling angry that the kite had broken.

qa.q: How could Baljeet keep helping Tanvir learn this skill?
qa.a: She can keep prompting the same bear hug and candle breaths, and slowly let Tanvir start them on his own.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Tanvir's calming down?
qa.a: She might feel happy and proud of her little brother for using words and breaths instead of a tantrum.

grounding: A young child uses a cuddly toy, candle breaths and the words "I am angry" to calm himself and feels proud.

passage:
"Himani, why is Arvind screaming?" Shankar whispered, holding the swing chain.
"He wanted the red scooter. Now he's on the floor."
"He kicked the scooter. I'm scared."
"Me too. Let's go stand by the wall."
"Should I make him stop?"
"No. That's the teacher's job. Come."
They ran to Mrs Pillai. "Arvind is very angry by the scooters!"
"Thank you both. I'll go to him."
After lunch, Shankar found Arvind by the water tap. "Want to share my orange?"
Arvind wiped his nose and nodded.

qa.q: Why was Arvind on the floor?
qa.a: He wanted the red scooter, and he was screaming on the floor.

qa.q: What was Shankar worried about when he asked if he should make Arvind stop?
qa.a: Shankar felt scared and unsure, and worried it was his job to fix Arvind's anger.

qa.q: Which choices did Shankar and Himani get right?
qa.a: They stepped back to the wall, told Mrs Pillai and let her handle it, then Shankar was kind to Arvind after lunch.

qa.q: How might Arvind feel when Shankar offers his orange?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and still liked, even after his big tantrum, and a little embarrassed.

grounding: Two young children feel scared by a friend's tantrum, step back and tell a teacher, and are kind to him later.

passage:
Note for Hrithik's mother, from his class teacher.
During painting, Elizabeth had a very big tantrum and tipped over the water pot. Hrithik froze with his brush in the air. He looked scared. Then he walked back to the reading corner, just like our class rule says, and came to tell me. I sat with Elizabeth until she was calm. Later I heard Hrithik ask her, "Do you want to paint the sun with me?" He asked me if Elizabeth was "broken". I told him big feelings pass. You may want to talk about it at bedtime. 🙂

qa.q: What did Elizabeth tip over during painting?
qa.a: Elizabeth tipped over the water pot.

qa.q: What does Hrithik asking if Elizabeth was "broken" suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt frightened and unsure, worried that Elizabeth's big feelings meant something was badly wrong with her.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that fits a wise response?
qa.a: He stepped back to the reading corner, told the teacher, and later invited Elizabeth to paint with him.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Hrithik's invitation to paint the sun?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and accepted, as if her friend still likes her after the tantrum.

grounding: A preschooler is scared by a friend's big tantrum, steps back, tells the teacher and is kind afterwards.

passage:
Friday: In the toy shop, Rehana hugged a talking parrot. "Ammi, please!" Her mother, Farida, said, "Not today." Rehana screamed and cried all the way to the bus. "You don't love me!" Farida stayed quiet and held her hand.
Saturday: Rehana drew a picture of the parrot with crayons. She kept looking at it.
The next Friday: They passed the shop again. Rehana stopped, took a breath and asked, "Can I have it on my birthday?" Farida smiled. "Let's write it on your birthday list." Rehana skipped to the bus.

qa.q: What toy did Rehana want in the shop?
qa.a: Rehana wanted a talking parrot.

qa.q: How was Rehana feeling when she shouted, "You don't love me!"?
qa.a: She was furious and hurt, and for that moment the no felt like her mother did not love her.

qa.q: What changed the second time, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rehana asked calmly if she could have it on her birthday, which gave Farida a real choice and got the parrot on a list without screaming.

qa.q: How might Farida feel when Rehana asks about her birthday?
qa.a: Farida probably feels proud and relieved that her daughter found a calm way to ask.

grounding: Over a week, a child moves from screaming at a parent's no to asking whether the toy could come on her birthday.

passage: The market was closing and Papa had only enough change left for the bus. Vasudha pointed at a shiny toy train. "Papa, buy it!" Deepak shook his head. "Not today, beta." Vasudha's face went hot. She felt Papa didn't love her at all. She opened her mouth to scream, the way she did when she wanted things. Then she saw the bus coming. She tugged Papa's sleeve instead. "Can I have it on my birthday?" Deepak squeezed her hand. "We'll ask for it then. Come, bus!" She looked back at the train, sighed and climbed on.

qa.q: Why couldn't Deepak buy the train that evening?
qa.a: Papa had only enough change left for the bus.

qa.q: How can you tell Vasudha was furious at first?
qa.a: Her face went hot, she felt Papa didn't love her, and she opened her mouth to scream the way she usually did.

qa.q: What did Vasudha try instead of screaming, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She asked if she could have the train on her birthday, which kept her wish alive without a fight.

qa.q: What is it like for Deepak when Vasudha tugs his sleeve instead of screaming?
qa.a: He feels relieved and proud; it lets him say yes to a plan even though he cannot say yes today.

grounding: A young child is furious at a parent's no to a toy but chooses to ask for it on her birthday instead of screaming.

passage:
Monday: "One more show, Mumma?" Zubin asked. "No, it's bath time." Zubin groaned and dragged his feet to the bathroom, grumbling the whole way.
Wednesday: "One more?" "Not tonight. Bath, then two stories." Zubin sighed, but he switched off the screen himself.
Sunday: Before Swati could say anything, Zubin clicked off the show. "Bath, then stories, right?" "Right," said Swati. Zubin stretched. "You always say no, but it's okay. Bath is warm anyway."

qa.q: What did Swati promise after the bath on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said bath, then two stories.

qa.q: What does Zubin switching off the show himself suggest he feels?
qa.a: He still feels a little grumpy, but he trusts that his mother's no is fair and that stories will come.

qa.q: Which part of Swati's approach built Zubin's trust?
qa.a: She gave the same kind no every night with a clear next step, so the rule felt steady instead of random.

qa.q: How might Swati feel on Sunday when Zubin switches off the show first?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and happy that the routine is working without a fight. 😊

grounding: Over a week, a child grumbles at a parent's no to more screen time but comes to trust and accept the rule.

passage: The power had gone out twice that evening, and the phone's battery was low. "One more show, Papa? Please?" Yamini begged. Ramesh shook his head. "No, kanna. We need the battery in case the lights stay off." Yamini pouted and crossed her arms. "Hmph." She kicked her pillow. Then she looked at Papa's face in the candlelight. Papa always had a reason. "Okay," she grumbled. "Can we make shadow animals instead?" Ramesh held up his hands and made a wobbly dog on the wall. Yamini giggled.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh want to save the phone battery?
qa.a: He said they needed the battery in case the lights stayed off.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she kicked her pillow?
qa.a: She felt cross and disappointed, but she still trusted that Papa had a reason.

qa.q: How could a parent make a no easier to trust, like Ramesh did?
qa.a: Give a short, kind reason and offer something else to do, such as shadow animals.

qa.q: What would change if Ramesh gave in because Yamini pouted?
qa.a: Yamini might learn that pouting works, and the battery could run out; the rule would feel less steady.

grounding: A child grumbles at a parent's no to another show but trusts there is a good reason and accepts it without a fight.

passage: At the swimming club, the whistle blew for the end of the lesson. "Out now, Tanvir," his dad, Farhan, called from the edge. "No! You're mean! I hate you!" Tanvir shouted, splashing. Then his eyes went wide. He climbed out and stood dripping, not looking up. Farhan wrapped him in the big towel. "You're angry. I still love you." Tanvir's chin wobbled. "Even when I said hate?" "Even then." In the changing room, Tanvir leaned against his dad's arm while his hair was dried.

qa.q: What did Farhan wrap Tanvir in?
qa.a: Farhan wrapped him in the big towel.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's eyes go wide after he shouted?
qa.a: He felt afraid of what he had said, worried that his hard words might end his dad's love, while still feeling angry.

qa.q: What did Farhan's reply teach Tanvir?
qa.a: By saying "You're angry. I still love you," he showed that hard words do not end love, without shouting back.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Tanvir says he hates him?
qa.a: It may sting, but Farhan understands it is anger talking, so he stays warm and steady.

grounding: A child shouts "I hate you" at a parent's no and feels scared by it, and the parent answers with calm love.

passage:
Tuesday: Maa said no to the park because of homework time. Usha yelled, "You're mean! I hate you!" and ran to her room. Under her blanket, she felt hot and shaky.
Wednesday: At breakfast, Usha would not look at Anirban, her father. He sat beside her. "You were angry yesterday. I still love you. So does Maa." Usha peeked out. "Even after hate?" "Even after."
Saturday: Maa said no to more ice cream. Usha scowled. "I'm angry at you." Then she hugged Maa's leg anyway.

qa.q: Why did Maa say no to the park on Tuesday?
qa.a: Maa said no because it was homework time.

qa.q: How was Usha feeling under her blanket?
qa.a: She felt angry and afraid at the same time, hot and shaky about the hard words she had shouted.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that helped?
qa.a: He sat beside Usha, named her anger and told her they both still loved her, so she learned hard words do not end love.

qa.q: How does Maa probably see Usha's hug on Saturday?
qa.a: She likely feels warm and relieved, seeing Usha can say she is angry and still stay close.

grounding: Over several days, a child learns that saying hard words in anger does not end her parents' love.
